sides.text: Approved secure configuration for a system type

more.text: A documented set of security settings every system of that type must meet (CIS Benchmarks, vendor guides). Process: establish, deploy, maintain.

sides.text: A company defines the standard settings every new server must have. What is it?

more.text: A secure baseline.
Create the baseline from standards and benchmarks (like CIS) and organizational policy, tailored to the system's role.

sides.text: Which step defines approved settings using CIS benchmarks?

more.text: Establish.
Roll the baseline out consistently with images, group policy, or configuration management tools.

sides.text: Gold images are used to build all new workstations. Which step?

more.text: Deploy.
Update the baseline for new threats and software, and monitor systems for drift from it.

sides.text: A scan finds servers that no longer match the approved settings. Which step addresses this?

more.text: Maintain: detect the drift and reapply the baseline.
Enforce screen lock, encryption, MDM enrollment, OS updates, app control, and remote wipe. Disable unneeded connectivity.

sides.text: Which tool enforces encryption and remote wipe on company phones?

more.text: MDM.
Patch, remove bloatware, enable the host firewall and endpoint protection, encrypt disks, use least privilege, and disable unneeded services.

sides.text: Which step reduces a workstation's attack surface by removing unneeded software?

more.text: Hardening: removing unnecessary software.
Disable unused ports, enable port security, change defaults, secure management (SSH, not Telnet), keep VLANs tidy, and use BPDU guard.

sides.text: Unused switch ports are shut down and placed in an unused VLAN. Why?

more.text: Hardening: it prevents unauthorized connections.
Change defaults, secure management access, disable unused services, apply ACLs, keep firmware current, and enable logging.

sides.text: A router's management interface is restricted to SSH from a management network.

more.text: Router hardening.
Least-privilege IAM, MFA, private storage by default, encryption, security groups, logging, and configuration monitoring.

sides.text: A cloud storage bucket must not be publicly readable. Which hardening step?

more.text: Restrict access and make it private.
Minimal installation, patching, disabling unneeded services and ports, secure remote access, logging, and baseline compliance.

sides.text: A server runs only the services its role needs. What is this?

more.text: Server hardening (minimal services).
Segment from IT networks, restrict remote access, monitor passively, patch cautiously, and control physical access.

sides.text: A plant's control network is separated from the corporate network. Why?

more.text: Hardening ICS/SCADA through isolation.
Change defaults, update firmware, disable unused interfaces, and segment from critical networks.

sides.text: A printer's default admin password is changed and its network access restricted.

more.text: Embedded system hardening.
Limit exposed services, restrict access, use secure boot where possible, and isolate. Patching may be constrained by timing and safety.

sides.text: A real-time controller can't be rebooted for patches. What's a hardening approach?

more.text: Isolate it and restrict access.
Change default credentials, update firmware, disable unneeded features, and place them on a separate VLAN.

sides.text: Smart sensors go on an isolated VLAN and their default passwords are changed.

more.text: IoT hardening.
A survey measures signal strength, interference, and coverage to place access points properly, avoiding dead zones and weak signal.

sides.text: Before deploying Wi-Fi, a team measures signal and interference throughout the building.

more.text: A site survey.
A floor plan colored by signal strength shows coverage gaps and overlap. Produced from a site survey.

sides.text: A colored floor plan shows weak Wi-Fi in the north wing. What is it?

more.text: A heat map.
Enforces policies on phones and tablets: encryption, passcodes, app controls, remote lock and wipe, and compliance checking.

sides.text: IT remotely wipes a lost company phone. Which tool?

more.text: MDM.
Employees use personal devices for work. Cheap, but harder to control and it mixes personal and corporate data. Use MDM and containerization.

sides.text: Staff use their own phones to read company email. Which model?

more.text: BYOD.
The company buys the device and allows personal use. Stronger control than BYOD, with a more employee-friendly experience.

sides.text: The company provides phones but lets staff use them personally. Which model?

more.text: COPE.
Employees choose from a company-approved list of devices that the company owns or manages. Balances choice and control.

sides.text: Employees pick from three approved laptops. Which model?

more.text: CYOD.
Cellular: carrier network, relatively secure. Wi-Fi: risky on public networks, so use a VPN. Bluetooth: pairing attacks like bluejacking and bluesnarfing, so disable it when unused.

sides.text: Which mobile connection is exposed to bluesnarfing?

more.text: Bluetooth.
Uses SAE for password-based authentication, replacing WPA2's PSK handshake. It resists offline dictionary attacks and provides forward secrecy. WPA3-Enterprise adds stronger encryption (GCMP-256).

sides.text: Which Wi-Fi standard resists offline password cracking using SAE?

more.text: WPA3.
Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service: centralized authentication, authorization, and accounting for network access, used with 802.1X for enterprise Wi-Fi and VPN.

sides.text: Enterprise Wi-Fi authenticates users against a central server. Which protocol?

more.text: RADIUS (with 802.1X).
WEP and TKIP are broken or deprecated. WPA2 uses AES-CCMP. WPA3 uses GCMP and SAE. Use WPA3, or WPA2-Enterprise.

sides.text:
Which Wi-Fi encryption protocol is considered broken:
WEP
AES-CCMP
GCMP?

more.text: WEP.
EAP types (EAP-TLS, PEAP), PAP (cleartext, weak), CHAP and MS-CHAP (challenge-response), and Kerberos (ticket-based). Prefer certificate-based methods like EAP-TLS.

sides.text:
Which protocol sends credentials in cleartext:
PAP
CHAP
Kerberos?

more.text: PAP.
Verify that input matches the expected type, length, and format. Prevents injection, XSS, and overflows. Validate on the server, not only the client.

sides.text: A form accepts only digits in a phone number field and rejects the rest on the server.

more.text: Input validation.
Set Secure (HTTPS only), HttpOnly (not readable by scripts), and SameSite attributes to reduce theft and CSRF.

sides.text: Which cookie flag stops JavaScript from reading a session cookie?

more.text: HttpOnly.

sides.text: Scan source code without running it

more.text: SAST finds flaws in source or binaries early in development, including injection patterns and hard-coded secrets. Can miss runtime issues.

sides.text: Developers scan source code for vulnerabilities before running it. Which technique?

more.text: Static code analysis (SAST).
Developers sign code with a private key so users can verify who published it and that it hasn't been altered.

sides.text: An installer shows a verified publisher and fails if tampered with. Which control?

more.text: Code signing.

sides.text: Run code in an isolated environment

more.text: Isolates untrusted programs so they can't affect the host. Used for testing malware, browsers, and mobile apps.

sides.text: A suspicious attachment is opened in an isolated environment to observe it.

more.text: Sandboxing.

sides.text: Observe systems and apps for security events

more.text: Continuous watching of logs, performance, and behavior to detect problems and verify controls.

sides.text: Which ongoing activity detects anomalies in application behavior?

more.text: Monitoring.

sides.text: Knowing and controlling what you own

more.text: Tracking hardware, software, and data across their lifecycle: acquisition, assignment, tracking, and disposal. You can't secure what you don't know exists.

sides.text: A team discovers servers nobody knew existed. Which practice was missing?

more.text: Asset management (an inventory).
Vet suppliers, define security requirements, verify authenticity, and approve purchases centrally to avoid shadow IT and counterfeit hardware.

sides.text: Purchases go through an approval process that checks vendor security. Which process?

more.text: Acquisition/procurement.

sides.text: Who is accountable for an asset

more.text: Each asset has an assigned owner responsible for it and its security.

sides.text: Every server has a named responsible person. Which concept?

more.text: Ownership.
Assets are classified (public, confidential, and so on) to decide protection and handling.

sides.text: A database is labeled confidential, so controls are chosen accordingly.

more.text: Classification.
An up-to-date record of hardware, software, and data, with owner and location. The foundation for patching and risk work.

sides.text: Which record lists every device and its owner?

more.text: An inventory.
Actively or passively identifying devices, services, and software, often through scans, to find unknown assets.

sides.text: A scan reveals unknown devices on the network. Which activity?

more.text: Enumeration.

sides.text: Removing data so it can't be recovered

more.text: Wiping, overwriting, degaussing, or cryptographic erase (destroying the encryption key) so data can't be recovered while the media may be reused.

sides.text: A drive is cryptographically erased and reused. Which process?

more.text: Sanitization.
Shredding, pulverizing, incinerating, or degaussing media so it can't be used. Used when sanitization isn't enough or media is retired.

sides.text: Hard drives from a retired server are shredded. Which method?

more.text: Destruction.
A certificate of destruction or sanitization documents that media was properly handled, supporting compliance and audits.

sides.text: A vendor provides paperwork proving drives were destroyed. What is it?

more.text: A certificate of destruction or sanitization.
Policies set how long data is kept to meet legal and business needs, then it's securely disposed of. Keeping data too long raises risk and cost.

sides.text: Which policy defines how long records must be kept before disposal?

more.text: The data retention policy.
Tools scan systems for missing patches, misconfigurations, and known vulnerabilities. Results need validation.

sides.text: A tool checks servers for missing patches and misconfigurations. Which activity?

more.text: A vulnerability scan.
Credentialed scans log in to hosts and see patches and settings accurately, with fewer false positives. Non-credentialed scans see what an outside attacker sees.

sides.text: A scan logs in to servers to check installed patches. Which type?

more.text: A credentialed scan.
Reviews source or compiled code for flaws before it runs (SAST). Finds issues early; may produce false positives.

sides.text: Which method finds flaws in code without executing it?

more.text: Static analysis.
Tests an application while it runs (DAST, fuzzing) to find runtime flaws such as injection and misconfiguration.

sides.text: A tester sends malformed input to a running app to find crashes. Which method?

more.text: Dynamic analysis (fuzzing).
Monitors third-party packages and dependencies for known vulnerabilities and malicious versions. Relevant to supply chain risk.

sides.text: A tool alerts that a library used in your app has a known flaw. Which activity?

more.text: Package monitoring.
Information from public sources: news, social media, vulnerability databases, and forums. Free and broad but needs validation.

sides.text: Analysts use public advisories and security blogs to learn of new threats. Which source?

more.text: OSINT.
Commercial feeds with curated, often more timely and actionable threat data. Costly but vetted.

sides.text: A company subscribes to a vendor's curated threat intelligence. Which source?

more.text: A proprietary/third-party feed.
ISACs and similar groups share threat intelligence among members in a sector, such as finance or healthcare.

sides.text: Banks share attack indicators through an industry group. What is it?

more.text: An information-sharing organization (ISAC).
Monitoring dark web forums and markets reveals stolen credentials, planned attacks, and data for sale.

sides.text: Monitoring finds company credentials for sale on underground forums.

more.text: Dark web intelligence.

A controlled attempt to exploit weaknesses to prove real risk. By knowledge level: known (white box), partially known (gray box), unknown (black box) environment. Requires written authorization and scope.

sides.text: A firm is hired to attack the network with permission and report findings. Which activity?

more.text: Penetration testing.
A policy that lets researchers report vulnerabilities privately, giving the vendor time to fix before public disclosure.

sides.text: A researcher privately reports a flaw and waits for the fix before publishing.

more.text: Responsible disclosure.
Pays researchers for valid vulnerabilities found within scope. Extends testing to many skilled people.

sides.text: A company pays outside researchers for the flaws they find. Which program?

more.text: A bug bounty.
A formal examination of systems, configurations, and processes against policy or standards to find gaps.

sides.text: An auditor checks whether systems follow documented procedures. Which activity?

more.text: A system/process audit.
Validate scan results before acting, to separate real vulnerabilities from false positives.

sides.text: An analyst manually checks whether a reported flaw actually exists. Which step?

more.text: Confirmation.
A scan or alert reports a vulnerability or attack that isn't real. Wastes time and causes alert fatigue.

sides.text: A scanner reports a flaw on a system that has already been patched. What is it?

more.text: A false positive.
A real vulnerability or attack is missed. More dangerous than a false positive because it creates false confidence.

sides.text: A scan misses an unpatched flaw that attackers later exploit. What is this?

more.text: A false negative.
Rank vulnerabilities by severity, exploitability, asset value, and exposure, rather than fixing everything at once.

sides.text: A team has 500 findings and limited time. What should it do first?

more.text: Prioritize by risk.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System: a 0 to 10 base score (Low, Medium, High, Critical) from exploitability and impact, adjusted by temporal and environmental factors.

sides.text: A flaw has a CVSS score of 9.8. How is it classed?

more.text: Critical severity.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: unique IDs (like CVE-2021-44228) for publicly known vulnerabilities, so everyone refers to the same flaw.

sides.text: What identifier names a specific publicly known vulnerability?

more.text: A CVE ID.
Grouping by type (injection, misconfiguration, outdated software) helps analysis, reporting, and trend spotting.

sides.text: Findings are grouped by flaw type for reporting. Which activity?

more.text: Vulnerability classification.

sides.text: Share of an asset's value lost

more.text: The percentage of an asset's value lost if a threat occurs. Used to compute single loss expectancy: SLE = asset value × exposure factor.

sides.text: An asset worth $100,000 would lose 40% in an incident. What's the exposure factor, and the SLE?

more.text: 40%, so the SLE is $40,000.
Factors specific to your environment, such as network exposure, compensating controls, and system criticality, that raise or lower a finding's real risk.

sides.text: A critical flaw is on an isolated internal server. How does that affect priority?

more.text: Environmental variables can lower its priority.
How a vulnerability affects the specific business or industry: regulation, reputation, safety, and revenue.

sides.text: A flaw affects regulated patient data. Which analysis factor raises priority?

more.text: Industry/organizational impact.

sides.text: How much risk the organization accepts

more.text: The level of risk leadership is willing to live with. Drives which findings get fixed and which are accepted.

sides.text: Management decides it will accept a low-severity finding. Which concept?

more.text: Risk tolerance.
Apply the vendor fix after testing. The primary remediation when a patch exists.

sides.text: A fix is available for a critical vulnerability. What's the best remediation?

more.text: Patching.
Cyber insurance transfers some financial loss from incidents. It doesn't fix the vulnerability.

sides.text: A company can't fix a flaw immediately and buys coverage for related losses. Which response?

more.text: Insurance (risk transference).
Isolate vulnerable systems to limit reach when patching isn't possible.

sides.text: A vulnerable system that can't be patched is isolated on its own VLAN.

more.text: Segmentation.
Other controls reduce risk when the primary fix isn't possible: isolation, extra monitoring, WAF rules.

sides.text: A WAF rule blocks exploitation of an unpatched web app. Which remediation?

more.text: A compensating control.
Documented, time-limited, risk-accepted approval to not fix or follow a requirement, with compensating controls and review.

sides.text: Management signs off on leaving a legacy system unpatched with extra monitoring.

more.text: An exception/exemption.
Re-run the scan to confirm the vulnerability is gone.

sides.text: After patching, a team scans again. Which step?

more.text: Rescanning.
A review that confirms fixes were applied and processes followed.

sides.text: An auditor checks records to confirm patches were applied.

more.text: Audit.

sides.text: Confirm the fix works as intended

more.text: Testing that the remediation works and didn't break anything.

sides.text: Testers confirm a patched application still works and is no longer exploitable.

more.text: Verification.
Summarize vulnerabilities, risk, remediation status, and trends for technical and management audiences.

sides.text: A monthly report summarizes open vulnerabilities for leadership.

more.text: Reporting.
Collect and analyze data from systems, applications, and infrastructure to detect problems and attacks early.

sides.text: Which activity gathers data from servers, apps, and network devices for security visibility?

more.text: Monitoring computing resources.
Centralizing logs from many sources so they can be searched and correlated, and protected from tampering.

sides.text: Logs from all servers are sent to one central platform. What is this?

more.text: Log aggregation.
Rules or analytics generate alerts for suspicious events so responders can act.

sides.text: A SIEM sends a notification after 20 failed logins. Which activity?

more.text: Alerting.
Routine vulnerability and compliance scans to find weaknesses and drift.

sides.text: Weekly scans identify new vulnerabilities. Which activity?

more.text: Scanning.
Dashboards and reports show trends, incidents, and compliance to teams and management.

sides.text: A report shows alert trends over a quarter.

more.text: Reporting.
Retaining logs for compliance and investigations after active use, protected for integrity.

sides.text: Logs must be kept for a year for audits. Which activity?

more.text: Archiving.
Analysts investigate an alert, determine if it's real, and respond or close it. Includes quarantine and tuning.

sides.text: An analyst checks whether an alert is a true positive. Which step?

more.text: Alert validation.
Move suspicious files or devices into isolation so they can't cause harm while they're investigated.

sides.text: Antivirus moves a suspicious file into a safe location. Which action?

more.text: Quarantine.
Adjust thresholds and rules so alerts are accurate and manageable, without hiding real threats.

sides.text: Too many false alarms are overwhelming analysts. What should be done?

more.text: Alert tuning.
Security Content Automation Protocol: standard formats for checking configuration and vulnerabilities and measuring compliance automatically.

sides.text: Which standard automates compliance and vulnerability checks?

more.text: SCAP.
Consensus configuration guides such as CIS Benchmarks and DISA STIGs, used to build baselines and measure compliance.

sides.text: Which resource provides recommended hardening settings for an OS?

more.text: A benchmark, such as CIS.
Agents give deep, continuous visibility on hosts but need deployment. Agentless collects remotely with less overhead but less depth.

sides.text: Software on each server reports logs continuously. Which approach?

more.text: Agent-based.
Security information and event management: aggregates logs, correlates events, alerts, and supports investigations and compliance.

sides.text: A platform correlates logs from firewalls, servers, and apps to spot attacks. Which tool?

more.text: A SIEM.
Scans files and behavior against signatures and heuristics to block and remove malware. Modern endpoint tools add behavior analysis.

sides.text: Software scans files for known malware signatures. Which tool?

more.text: Antivirus.
Data loss prevention inspects and blocks sensitive data in email, web traffic, endpoints, and cloud services.

sides.text: A tool blocks an email containing credit card numbers. Which tool?

more.text: DLP.

sides.text: Devices send alerts to a manager

more.text: SNMP agents on devices send unsolicited trap messages to a management station when events occur. Use SNMPv3 for security.

sides.text: A switch alerts the monitoring server when a port fails. Which mechanism?

more.text: An SNMP trap.
Summarizes network conversations (source, destination, ports, volume) for traffic analysis and anomaly detection, without full packet content.

sides.text: Analysts review who talked to whom and how much data moved. Which data source?

more.text: NetFlow.
Tools like Nessus and OpenVAS scan for known weaknesses and report findings.

sides.text: Which tool automatically checks hosts for known vulnerabilities?

more.text: A vulnerability scanner.

sides.text: Allow or deny traffic by criteria

more.text: Rules match source, destination, port, and protocol, then permit or deny. Processed top-down with the first match winning, ending in an implicit deny. Keep rules specific and reviewed.

sides.text: Which firewall behavior denies anything not explicitly permitted?

more.text: The implicit deny.
Lists of permit and deny entries on routers and firewalls, applied to interfaces. Order matters: specific rules before general ones. They end with an implicit deny.

sides.text: A router ACL permits web traffic and drops everything else. What ends the list?

more.text: An implicit deny.

sides.text: Control services by port and protocol

more.text: Allow only needed ports and protocols (443, 22) and block risky ones (23, 21, and 445 from the internet). This is least functionality.

sides.text: A firewall allows only TCP 443 to the web server. Which principle?

more.text: Allowing only required ports and protocols.
Firewall rules let the internet reach public servers in the subnet and strictly limit what those servers can reach inside.

sides.text: A public web server should reach the internal database on one port only. Where is it placed, and how is it limited?

more.text: In a screened subnet, with firewall rules allowing only that port.
Analysis of alert trends (spikes, repeated sources) helps tune detection, find stealthy campaigns, and spot false positives.

sides.text: Analysts see repeated alerts from the same subnet every night. What does this reveal?

more.text: A trend that may indicate persistent activity, or a rule needing tuning.

Signature-based detection matches traffic to known attack patterns: accurate for known threats, blind to new ones. Anomaly-based detection finds deviations from normal but produces more false positives.

sides.text: A system detects only attacks it has patterns for. Which detection method?

more.text: Signature-based.

sides.text: Software on the device enforces filtering

more.text: An agent on the endpoint enforces web policy anywhere, including off the corporate network. Needs deployment and updates.

sides.text: Laptops are filtered even at home because software is installed on them. Which type?

more.text: An agent-based web filter.

sides.text: Gateway filters traffic for all users

more.text: All web traffic passes through a central proxy that applies policy, logs, and can inspect TLS. Off-network users must route through it.

sides.text: All office web traffic passes through one gateway that applies policies. Which type?

more.text: A centralized proxy.
Evaluates URLs against lists and live analysis to block malicious destinations.

sides.text: A link in an email is checked against a database of malicious sites before it opens.

more.text: URL scanning.
Sites are classified (gambling, social media, malware) so policy can allow or block whole categories.

sides.text: Policy blocks the gambling category. Which filter feature?

more.text: Content categorization.
Specific rules that block named sites, categories, or file types. They complement allow lists.

sides.text: A rule blocks a known malicious domain. What is it?

more.text: A block rule.

sides.text: Trust score for sites and senders

more.text: Sites, IPs, and domains are scored by history; low-reputation destinations are blocked or flagged.

sides.text: A newly registered domain with a poor history is blocked. Which feature?

more.text: Reputation-based filtering.
A Windows Active Directory feature that pushes security settings (password rules, firewall, restrictions) to computers and users centrally.

sides.text: An admin enforces password rules on all domain computers from one place. Which tool?

more.text: Group Policy.
Security-Enhanced Linux enforces mandatory access control policies on processes and files, limiting damage from compromised services. Modes: enforcing, permissive, disabled.

sides.text: A Linux system confines processes with mandatory access policies. Which feature?

more.text: SELinux.
Pick protocols that provide encryption and authentication: SSH over Telnet, HTTPS over HTTP, SFTP over FTP.

sides.text: Which protocol should replace FTP for secure file transfer?

more.text: SFTP (or FTPS).
Use standard secure ports (443, 22, 636) and close insecure ones. Changing ports adds little security by itself.

sides.text: How the protocol is secured in transit

more.text: Secure via TLS wrapping, a STARTTLS upgrade, or VPN/IPsec tunnels. Choose the method that fits the application.

sides.text: An email session starts in plaintext and upgrades to encrypted. Which method?

more.text: STARTTLS.
DNS resolvers refuse or redirect lookups for malicious or unwanted domains, stopping phishing, malware, and command-and-control early.

sides.text: Lookups for known malware domains return no answer. Which control?

more.text: DNS filtering.
Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance: builds on SPF and DKIM, tells receivers what to do with failures (none, quarantine, reject), and sends reports.

sides.text: A domain owner tells receivers to reject mail that fails SPF and DKIM alignment. Which control?

more.text: DMARC.
DomainKeys Identified Mail: the sending server signs messages, and receivers verify with a public key in DNS to confirm the domain and that the content wasn't altered.

sides.text: Receivers verify an email's signature using a public key in DNS. Which control?

more.text: DKIM.

sides.text: Lists servers allowed to send for a domain

more.text: Sender Policy Framework: a DNS record listing authorized sending servers. Receivers check the sending IP against it to detect spoofing.

sides.text: A DNS record lists which mail servers may send for a domain. Which control?

more.text: SPF.
Scans email for spam, phishing, malware, and sensitive data, and enforces policy before mail reaches users.

sides.text: Inbound mail is scanned for malware and phishing before delivery. Which control?

more.text: An email gateway.
FIM compares files to known-good hashes and alerts on changes to critical system and config files. Helps detect tampering and meet compliance.

sides.text: An alert fires when a system file's hash changes unexpectedly. Which tool?

more.text: File integrity monitoring.
Inspects data in motion, at rest, and in use against policy, and blocks, encrypts, or alerts on leaks across email, endpoints, and cloud.

sides.text: A policy blocks uploading files with Social Security numbers to personal cloud storage.

more.text: DLP.
Network access control authenticates devices and checks posture before granting access, quarantining non-compliant ones.

sides.text: A device lacking antivirus is placed in a remediation VLAN. Which technology?

more.text: NAC.
Continuously monitors endpoint behavior, records activity, detects threats, and enables investigation and response such as isolation and remediation.

sides.text: A tool records process behavior on laptops and can isolate an infected one. Which tool?

more.text: EDR.
Extends EDR by correlating data across endpoints, network, email, and cloud for broader detection and response.

sides.text: A platform correlates telemetry from endpoints, email, and network to detect attacks. Which tool?

more.text: XDR.
UBA baselines normal user and entity behavior and flags anomalies, such as odd login times or mass downloads, to detect insider threats and stolen credentials.

sides.text: A tool flags an employee downloading far more files than usual. Which technology?

more.text: User behavior analytics.
Provisioning: creating accounts and assigning access when someone joins or changes role. De-provisioning: removing access promptly when they leave. Delays leave orphaned accounts.

sides.text: A departed employee's account is still active a month later. What failed?

more.text: De-provisioning.
Excess permissions cause privilege creep, so grant least privilege and review regularly. Roles and groups simplify assignment.

sides.text: A long-time employee has accumulated access from several past roles. What is this?

more.text: Privilege creep.

sides.text: Verify a person is who they claim

more.text: Confirming real-world identity before creating an account or credential: documents, knowledge checks, in-person verification.

sides.text: A new user must show government ID to get an account. Which process?

more.text: Identity proofing.
Lets users from one organization authenticate to another's services with their home credentials, via standards like SAML and OpenID Connect.

sides.text: Employees log in to a partner's portal with their own company credentials. Which concept?

more.text: Federation.
Authenticate once and access multiple apps. Reduces password fatigue, but it's a high-value target, so protect it with MFA.

sides.text: A user logs in once and opens several apps without logging in again.

more.text: Single sign-on (SSO).
Lightweight Directory Access Protocol: queries and updates directory services like Active Directory. LDAPS secures it with TLS (port 636).

sides.text: Applications look up users in a central directory. Which protocol?

more.text: LDAP (LDAPS when secured).
Open authorization: lets an app access resources on a user's behalf using tokens, without sharing the password. It's authorization, not authentication.

sides.text: A photo app is allowed to read your cloud files without your password. Which protocol?

more.text: OAuth.
Security Assertions Markup Language: an identity provider sends signed XML assertions to a service provider for SSO. Common for enterprise web apps.

sides.text: An identity provider sends a signed assertion to a cloud app to log you in. Which standard?

more.text: SAML.
Identity systems and standards need to work across platforms; lack of it causes gaps and workarounds.

sides.text: Two identity systems can't exchange authentication data. What's lacking?

more.text: Interoperability.
Verification that a device or software is in a trusted state (such as secure boot attestation), or confirmation by managers that users' access is still appropriate (access recertification).

sides.text: A manager periodically confirms that team members still need their access. Which activity?

more.text: Attestation (an access review).
A KDC issues tickets (a TGT, then service tickets), so passwords aren't sent over the network. Requires synchronized time. Used in Active Directory.

sides.text: A ticket granting ticket is issued after login. Which protocol?

more.text: Kerberos.
OIDC adds identity (authentication) to OAuth's authorization using ID tokens. Used for sign in with another provider.

sides.text: A site lets you log in using your account from another provider, via ID tokens.

more.text: OpenID Connect.

sides.text: Labels and clearances set by the system

more.text: Access follows sensitivity labels and user clearances enforced by the system; users can't override. Used in high-security environments.

sides.text: Files are labeled Secret and only users cleared for Secret can read them. Which model?

more.text: MAC.
The resource owner decides who gets access, usually through ACLs. Flexible but weaker control.

sides.text: A file's creator grants a coworker read access. Which model?

more.text: DAC.
Permissions are tied to job roles; users get access through role membership. Simplifies administration and supports least privilege.

sides.text: All nurses get the same record permissions through a Nurse role. Which model?

more.text: RBAC.
Access decisions follow fixed rules set by an administrator, such as allow/deny conditions or time-of-day limits, rather than the user's role.

sides.text: Access is allowed only from corporate IP ranges, enforced by system rules. Which model?

more.text: Rule-based access control.
Decisions evaluate attributes of the user, resource, and context (department, device, location, time) against policy. Highly granular.

sides.text: Access depends on the user's department, the data's sensitivity, and the device. Which model?

more.text: ABAC.
Accounts can log in only during permitted hours, reducing the risk of misuse after hours.

sides.text: Contractors can log in only between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. Which control?

more.text: Time-of-day restrictions.
Give accounts the minimum permissions to do the job, and review regularly. Limits damage from compromise.

sides.text: A help desk technician needs to reset passwords but not change firewall rules. Which principle?

more.text: Least privilege.
Combines different factor types (know, have, are, somewhere you are). Two of the same type isn't MFA. Stops most credential-theft attacks.

sides.text: A password plus a fingerprint scan. Is this MFA?

more.text: Yes: knowledge plus inherence.
Fingerprint, face, iris, voice. Convenient but can't be changed if compromised. Measured by FAR, FRR, and the crossover error rate (CER).

sides.text: Which biometric measure is the point where the false accept and false reject rates are equal?

more.text: The crossover error rate (CER).
False acceptance rate: unauthorized users let in (a security risk). False rejection rate: authorized users blocked (a usability cost). Lower crossover error is better.

sides.text: A biometric lets an unauthorized person in. Which error?

more.text: A false acceptance.
Hard tokens: physical devices generating codes. Soft tokens: authenticator apps. TOTP codes change every 30 seconds; HOTP codes are counter-based.

sides.text: An app shows a code that changes every 30 seconds. Which type?

more.text: A soft token (TOTP).
Hardware devices using FIDO2/WebAuthn public-key cryptography. Resistant to phishing since they verify the site.

sides.text: A USB key is tapped to approve a login and can't be phished. What is it?

more.text: A security key (FIDO2).
Password, PIN, or answer. Can be guessed, stolen, or phished.
Something you know.
Phone, smart card, token, or key. Can be lost or stolen.

sides.text: A smart card is which factor?

more.text: Something you have.
Biometric traits: fingerprint, face, iris.

sides.text: A face scan is which factor?

more.text: Something you are.
Location context such as GPS, IP geolocation, or network location, used as an additional signal.

sides.text: Access is allowed only from the office network. Which factor?

more.text: Somewhere you are.
Favor length over complexity, avoid reuse, use a password manager, add MFA, and check against breached lists. Current guidance discourages frequent forced rotation without cause.

sides.text: Which matters most for password strength: length or frequent rotation?

more.text: Length.
Each added character multiplies the guesses needed. Passphrases of 14 or more characters are strong and memorable.

sides.text: Which change most increases brute-force resistance?

more.text: Increasing length.
Requiring upper case, lower case, digits, and symbols raises entropy but leads to predictable patterns. Length matters more.

sides.text: A rule requires mixed character types. Which concept?

more.text: Complexity.
Reusing passwords lets one breach compromise many accounts (credential stuffing). Password history policies prevent reusing old ones.

sides.text: Attackers log in to many sites with passwords leaked from one site. What is this?

more.text: Credential stuffing, enabled by reuse.

sides.text: Passwords must change after a time

more.text: Forces periodic change. Modern guidance (NIST) favors changing only on compromise, since forced rotation produces weaker passwords.

sides.text: A policy forces changes every 90 days. Which concept?

more.text: Password expiration.
Minimum age stops users cycling through changes to reuse an old password immediately; maximum age forces eventual change.

sides.text: Users can't change a password again for a day. Which setting?

more.text: Minimum password age.
Encrypted vaults generate and store unique passwords and autofill only on correct sites, reducing reuse and phishing.

sides.text: A tool creates and stores a unique password per site. What is it?

more.text: A password manager.
Uses passkeys, biometrics, security keys, or magic links with public-key cryptography. Removes password theft and phishing.

sides.text: Users sign in with a device-bound passkey and a fingerprint. Which approach?

more.text: Passwordless authentication.
Tools that secure privileged accounts: vaulting credentials, granting time-limited access, recording sessions, and enforcing least privilege.

sides.text: Admins check out credentials from a vault and sessions are recorded. Which solution?

more.text: PAM.

sides.text: Access only when needed, then removed

more.text: Elevated rights are granted temporarily for a task and revoked automatically, shrinking standing privileges.

sides.text: An admin gets elevated rights for two hours, then they expire. Which approach?

more.text: Just-in-time permissions.
Credentials are stored encrypted, checked out under policy, logged, and rotated automatically.

sides.text: Privileged passwords are stored in a secure vault and rotated after use.

more.text: Password vaulting.
Credentials that exist briefly and expire automatically, so stolen ones quickly become useless.

sides.text: A credential is generated for one session and expires after use. Which type?

more.text: An ephemeral credential.
Scripts or workflows create, change, and disable accounts when HR events occur, ensuring speed and consistency.

sides.text: A new hire's accounts are created automatically from the HR system. Which use case?

more.text: User provisioning.
Automatically build servers, networks, and cloud resources from templates (IaC) with consistent security settings.

sides.text: A script builds a hardened server from a template. Which use case?

more.text: Resource provisioning.

sides.text: Automated limits that prevent unsafe actions

more.text: Policies that block or flag risky actions automatically, such as preventing public storage buckets or disallowed regions.

sides.text: A cloud policy automatically blocks creating public storage. Which concept?

more.text: Guard rails.
Automating the creation and updating of security group rules keeps access consistent and least-privilege.

sides.text: Rules are updated automatically when a new server is added. Which use case?

more.text: Automating security groups.
Alerts automatically create tickets with context so issues are tracked and assigned.

sides.text: A SIEM alert opens a ticket with details automatically.

more.text: Ticket creation automation.
Unresolved or severe alerts are automatically escalated to senior staff within set time limits.

sides.text: A critical alert that isn't acknowledged in 15 minutes pages the on-call manager.

more.text: Escalation.

sides.text: Enabling and disabling services and access

more.text: Automatically turn services or accounts on or off in response to events, such as disabling a compromised account.

sides.text: A compromised account is automatically disabled after a risk alert.

more.text: Automated disabling of access.
CI/CD pipelines build code and run automated security tests (SAST, dependency scans) on every change, catching flaws early.

sides.text: Every code commit triggers automated security scans. Which practice?

more.text: Continuous integration and testing.
APIs let security tools share data and trigger actions, enabling orchestration across systems. APIs themselves must be secured.

sides.text: A SOAR tool calls a firewall API to block an IP automatically. Which capability?

more.text: Integration through APIs.
Automation frees staff from routine tasks, reducing delays and errors.

sides.text: Automating account creation saves hours each week. Which benefit?

more.text: Efficiency/time saving.
Automation applies and reapplies secure configurations, correcting drift.

sides.text: A tool restores required settings whenever they change. Which benefit?

more.text: Enforcing baselines.
Templates and scripts build systems the same way every time, reducing misconfiguration.

sides.text: All servers are built from one template. Which benefit?

more.text: Standard infrastructure configurations.
Automation applies security controls as systems scale, instead of requiring manual work for each new system.

sides.text: New cloud instances get security settings automatically as they scale.

more.text: Scaling in a secure manner.
Removing repetitive tasks lets staff do more meaningful work, which can improve morale and retention.

sides.text: Which benefit comes from freeing analysts from repetitive tasks?

more.text: Employee retention.
Automated response acts in seconds, limiting damage from attacks.

sides.text: A system blocks a malicious IP in seconds without human action. Which benefit?

more.text: Faster reaction time.

sides.text: Do more with the same team

more.text: Automation lets a small team handle more systems and alerts, effectively multiplying capacity.

sides.text: One analyst handles alerts that once needed several people. Which benefit?

more.text: Workforce multiplier.
Automation adds scripts, integrations, and dependencies that can be hard to understand and troubleshoot.

sides.text: A chain of scripts is hard to understand. Which concern?

more.text: Complexity.
Licenses, development time, and maintenance cost money; make sure the return justifies it.

sides.text: Which consideration weighs tool licensing and engineering time?

more.text: Cost.
If the automation platform fails or is wrong, many processes fail. Build in redundancy and fallback.

sides.text: A failed orchestration server stops all incident response. Which risk?

more.text: A single point of failure.
Quick fixes and undocumented scripts accumulate and make future changes harder and riskier.

sides.text: Old undocumented scripts nobody dares change. Which concept?

more.text: Technical debt.
Automation needs updates, monitoring, documentation, and skilled owners over time.

sides.text: Which consideration covers who will maintain scripts in future years?

more.text: Ongoing supportability.
Automation performs a task. Orchestration coordinates multiple automated tasks and systems into a workflow. SOAR platforms orchestrate security response.

sides.text: A platform ties alerts, enrichment, and blocking into one workflow. Which concept?

more.text: Orchestration (SOAR).
Preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned. Follow the plan in order.

sides.text: Which phase comes right after detection?

more.text: Analysis.
Develop the IR plan, assemble a team, train, and set up tools and communication channels.

sides.text: A team writes a plan and sets up tools before any incident. Which phase?

more.text: Preparation.
Identify events through monitoring, alerts, and reports to recognize that an incident may be occurring.

sides.text: A SIEM alert reveals unusual outbound traffic. Which phase?

more.text: Detection.
Determine scope, severity, and impact: what's affected, how it entered, what the attacker did.

sides.text: An analyst determines which systems are affected and how the attacker got in. Which phase?

more.text: Analysis.
Limit damage by isolating affected systems or accounts, short term and long term, while preserving evidence.

sides.text: Infected hosts are disconnected from the network. Which phase?

more.text: Containment.
Eliminate the threat: remove malware, close the entry point, reset credentials, and patch vulnerabilities.

sides.text: The malware is removed and the exploited flaw is patched. Which phase?

more.text: Eradication.
Bring systems back safely from clean backups and monitor for reinfection.

sides.text: Systems are rebuilt from clean backups and returned to service. Which phase?

more.text: Recovery.
After the incident, review what happened, what worked, and what to change; update plans and controls.

sides.text: A post-incident meeting identifies improvements. Which phase?

more.text: Lessons learned.
Regular training ensures staff know their roles and the plan, including exercises and awareness of reporting procedures.

sides.text: Staff practice their incident roles each quarter. Which activity?

more.text: Training.

sides.text: Walk through a scenario in discussion

more.text: A discussion-based test of the IR plan with no systems touched. Reveals gaps cheaply.

sides.text: Leaders discuss how they'd respond to a breach scenario in a meeting.

more.text: A tabletop exercise.
A realistic simulated incident (red and blue team, live drills) tests people, processes, and tools.

sides.text: A simulated attack tests detection and response by the SOC.

more.text: A simulation.
Determine the underlying cause, not just the symptoms, so it can be fixed and not recur.

sides.text: After an outage, a team traces it to a missed patch process. Which activity?

more.text: Root cause analysis.
Analysts actively look for signs of compromise that alerts missed, using hypotheses and threat intelligence.

sides.text: Analysts search logs for signs of an attacker before any alert fires. Which activity?

more.text: Threat hunting.
A directive to retain relevant data and suspend normal deletion when litigation or an investigation is expected.

sides.text: Legal tells IT to stop deleting emails related to a lawsuit. What is this?

more.text: A legal hold.
A record of who collected, handled, and stored evidence and when, proving it wasn't altered. Required for it to be admissible.

sides.text: Every person who handled a drive signs a log. What is it?

more.text: Chain of custody.
Collect data (disk images, memory, logs) using forensically sound methods such as write blockers and hashing to preserve integrity.

sides.text: An investigator images a drive using a write blocker and hashes it. Which step?

more.text: Acquisition.
A clear, accurate report of what was collected, how, and what was found, suitable for management or legal use.

sides.text: An investigator documents methods and conclusions for the legal team. Which step?

more.text: Reporting.
Protect evidence from change or loss through hashing, secure storage, and limited access.

sides.text: Evidence is hashed and locked in a secure room. Which step?

more.text: Preservation.

sides.text: Finding electronic evidence for legal cases

more.text: Identifying, collecting, and producing electronic information for legal proceedings, under legal hold.

sides.text: Lawyers request relevant emails and documents for a case. Which process?

more.text: E-discovery.

sides.text: Collect the most fleeting data first

more.text: Capture from most to least volatile: CPU registers and cache, RAM, network state and processes, then disk, then logs and backups.

sides.text: Which should be collected first: a disk image or RAM?

more.text: RAM, because it's more volatile.
Show source, destination, port, protocol, and action. Useful for spotting scans, blocked attacks, and unusual outbound traffic.

sides.text: Which logs show a blocked connection attempt from an external IP?

more.text: Firewall logs.
Record application events, errors, and user actions, such as failed logins or SQL errors, to help investigate attacks on apps.

sides.text: Which logs show repeated SQL errors from a web app?

more.text: Application logs.
Record process starts, file changes, and USB use on endpoints. Key for tracing malware.

sides.text: Which logs show a process starting on a workstation?

more.text: Endpoint logs.
The Windows Security log (logons, privilege use) and Linux auth logs show authentication and access events.

sides.text: Which logs show failed administrator logons on a Windows server?

more.text: OS-specific security logs.
Alerts on signatures matched and traffic blocked or flagged, with details of the source and rule.

sides.text: Which logs show a detected exploit attempt and the matching signature?

more.text: IDS/IPS logs.
From routers, switches, DNS, DHCP, and proxies. Show who connected to what and when.

sides.text: Which logs show which device had a given IP at a given time?

more.text: Network logs (DHCP).
Information about files, emails, and traffic (author, timestamps, headers, geolocation) that helps establish when and who, without needing content.

sides.text: Email headers reveal the originating server. What is that information?

more.text: Metadata.
Scan results show unpatched or exposed systems and help determine how an attacker got in.

sides.text: Which source shows that a compromised server had a known unpatched flaw?

more.text: Vulnerability scan results.
Regular reports from tools summarize security events and trends to support investigation and oversight.

sides.text: A weekly summary shows spikes in failed logins. Which source?

more.text: Automated reports.
Visual displays of key metrics and alerts (SIEM dashboards) for quick monitoring and trend spotting.

sides.text: A wall display shows live security alerts and trends. What is it?

more.text: A dashboard.
Full packet data (pcap, Wireshark) allows deep analysis of what actually crossed the network, including payloads. Large and sensitive.

sides.text: Which source reveals the actual contents of network communications?

more.text: Packet captures.
Correlation links events from multiple logs to reveal an attack sequence that no single log shows. Needs synchronized time (NTP).

sides.text: A login failure on a server, a firewall block, and a data transfer are linked as one attack. What is this?

more.text: Event correlation in the SIEM.
